title: The Wedding Before the Dream
description: In an ancient legal household in Lucknow, wildlife biologist Divya Shukla has hidden her binoculars beneath her bridal silks for four years—until her husband Madhav rents an old Mahindra Thar, invents a fictitious land dispute, and drives her into the mist of Dudhwa National Park to confront what their marriage was meant to be.
excerpt: The courtyard clock in Qaiserbagh struck the quarter-hour with a heavy, bronze gong that made the water in the copper tumblers tremble on the breakfast tray.
author: Noble John Steeven
coverImageAlt: A pair of heavy black field binoculars resting on a dark teak writing desk beside legal leather-bound volumes, morning light filtering through a high arched Lucknow jali window

storySections.heading: I. The Clock in Qaiserbagh
storySections.body:
The courtyard clock in Qaiserbagh struck the quarter-hour with a heavy, bronze gong that made the water in the copper tumblers tremble on the breakfast tray.

It was an English grandfather clock, seven feet tall, imported from Birmingham in 1904 by Madhav's great-grandfather, a district judge under the colonial administration. It stood in the central lightwell of the hundred-and-twenty-year-old brick house, its pendulum swinging with the slow, implacable rhythm of an institution that had survived two world wars, the abolition of the zamindari system, and three generations of legal reform without ever speeding up or slowing down.

Divya stood at the marble kitchen counter, slicing almonds into eight identical porcelain saucers.

She was twenty-nine. She was wearing a plum-colored cotton handloom saree with a dull gold border, the pallu pinned to her left shoulder with a silver safety pin her mother-in-law had given her on her wedding day. Her hair was gathered into a low, sensible chignon at the nape of her neck.

On her wrists were two thin gold bangles. When her hands moved against the wooden chopping board, the gold clicked with a dry, metallic punctuation: *click, tap, click, tap*.

Below in the outer chamber—the *baithak*—eight junior advocates were already assembling for the morning conference. They were young men in ill-fitting black coats, fresh out of Lucknow University's law faculty, clutching pink paper briefs tied with white cotton tape. They spoke in hushed, reverent murmurs, waiting for Pandit Ramakant Shukla—Madhav's father, senior advocate at the High Court, former president of the Oudh Bar Association—to descend the wooden staircase.

Every morning between 7:30 and 8:15, Divya performed the ritual.

Eight cups of sweet tea made with full-cream milk and crushed green cardamom. Eight saucers of slivered almonds. Two toasted slices of white bread with salted butter for Pandit-ji.

She had performed this choreography one thousand four hundred and sixty times.

Four years earlier, when she had married Madhav, she had possessed two steel trunks. One trunk contained her bridal trousseau: the heavy Banarasi brocades, the embroidered chiffon dupattas, the gold jewelry wrapped in red velvet pouches.

The other trunk contained her life.

In that second trunk were sixteen field notebooks bound in water-resistant olive fabric; forty-two 1:50,000 Survey of India topographical sheets marked with red contour tracings; two GPS handheld receivers with scratched LCD screens; an incomplete M.Phil thesis titled *Spatial Dynamics and Corridors of Cervus duvaucelii in the Terai Floodplain Ecosystem*; and a pair of heavy Nikon 10x42 Monarch field binoculars.

The binoculars had been a gift from her advisor at the Wildlife Institute of India in Dehradun.

When she had moved into the Qaiserbagh house, her mother-in-law, Nirmala Devi, had inspected the bedroom wardrobe. With gentle, devastating politeness—the kind of ancient Awadhi courtesy that cuts more cleanly than a razor—Nirmala Devi had moved the olive notebooks and the black binoculars to the bottom shelf, behind the folded winter quilts.

'In this house, beti,' Nirmala Devi had said, smoothing the velvet border of a quilt, 'men practice the law, and women protect the household. Your father is a distinguished professor, but here, Ramakant-ji's clients expect to see a daughter-in-law who honors the threshold.'

Divya had said nothing. She had bowed her head, touched her mother-in-law's feet, and pushed the black binoculars into the dark corner behind the wool.

For four years, the binoculars had remained there. Sometimes, in the middle of the night, when the grandfather clock chimed 3:00 AM and Madhav was asleep beside her with his arm heavy across her waist, Divya would slide out of bed, open the wardrobe door, reach into the darkness behind the quilts, and rest her fingertips against the cold, textured rubber of the barrels.

She did not take them out. She merely touched them, verifying that the world she had known—the smell of wet elephant grass at sunrise, the sharp alarm call of a hog deer across a swamp, the freezing mist of the northern forests—had not been an illusion she had dreamed before her wedding.

storySections.heading: II. The Junior Advocate's Ledger
storySections.body:
Madhav Shukla sat at the corner table of the *baithak*, examining a title deed from 1968 concerning sixteen bighas of disputed orchard land in Sitapur.

He was thirty-one. He wore a dark grey coat that had belonged to his father twenty years earlier, taken in at the shoulders by a tailor in Aminabad. He was a competent lawyer—meticulous, patient, with an instinct for statutory precedents that earned him the quiet respect of the older judges on Bench Three.

His father, Pandit Ramakant Shukla, sat at the head of the long teak table beneath a framed portrait of Motilal Nehru.

Ramakant-ji was sixty-two, with a mane of white hair that fell to his collar and a voice like a bronze church bell. He was explaining the finer points of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act to a terrified junior from Hardoi, his fountain pen tapping the mahogany with rhythmic authority.

Madhav was not listening to his father.

He was looking through the open teak door into the lightwell.

Divya was coming down the three steps from the pantry, carrying the brass tray with eight steaming cups. She walked with a strange, flat-footed stiffness—the posture of a woman who had trained her body to occupy as little space as possible.

When they had met in 2019 at a mutual family wedding in Allahabad, she had not walked this way.

He remembered her walking along the rocky riverbank at Sangam in a pair of scuffed hiking boots, her canvas tote bag slung over one shoulder, pointing out the winter migratory birds to a cluster of bored children with an energy so vivid, so fierce and electric, that he had stood behind a temple pillar for half an hour simply watching her face.

When he had told his father he wanted to marry her, Ramakant-ji had hesitated. *'She is an academic's daughter, Madhav. Those girls from Dehradun have strange ideas about independence.'*

Madhav had insisted. *'She is brilliant, Babuji. And she is kind.'*

She was kind. That was the tragedy of it. Divya was too gentle, too respectful of his parents' dignity to scream, or throw plates, or make a scene in the courtyard. Instead, she had simply complied. She had laid her mind upon the altar of their respectability and watched it burn to ash in eight-ounce teacups.

At dinner two nights earlier, Madhav had watched her hands while she served the yellow arhar dal.

Those hands had once held radiotelemetry antennas in the swamp forests of the Nepal border. They had mapped animal movement through monsoonal marshes where tigers hunted in the high reed beds. Now, those hands were shaking slightly as she tried to pour the hot lentil soup without splashing the rim of Ramakant-ji's brass bowl.

Ramakant-ji had not noticed. He had been talking about an injunction matter before the Chief Justice.

Madhav had looked at Divya's eyes. There was no anger in them. There was something infinitely worse: there was a vacant, grey submission—the quiet extinction of a wild creature that has stopped pacing against the bars because it has forgotten that the forest exists.

Madhav closed the Sitapur file. He set his pen down.

He felt a sudden, sharp knot of shame tighten in his throat.

He had promised to protect her. In Allahabad, under the marigold canopy of the wedding mandap, with the sacred fire crackling between them, he had taken seven vows to share her life, her dreams, and her burdens. Instead, he had brought her into this mausoleum of legal briefs, closed the doors, and asked her to be a spectator at his father's monument.

He stood up from the table.

'Babuji,' Madhav said, his voice cutting through the junior's halting presentation on agricultural leases.

Ramakant-ji looked up over his half-moon reading spectacles, his brow furrowing. 'Yes, Madhav?'

'The partition suit in Lakhimpur Kheri,' Madhav said, inventing the client on the spot with the quick, reckless improvisation of an advocate under cross-examination. 'The revenue records from 1952 are missing from the district collectorate. The client has the original settlement papers at his village near Palia Kalan. If we don't inspect the boundary pillars in person before Monday, the sub-divisional magistrate will dismiss our stay petition.'

Ramakant-ji frowned. 'Palia Kalan? That is four hours past Sitapur, near the Nepal border. Why send you? Send an advocate commissioner.'

'The stakes are forty lakhs, Babuji,' Madhav lied, looking straight into his father's eyes. 'The other side has engaged Mishra-ji from the Lucknow bench. I must inspect the site myself.'

Ramakant-ji stared at his son for five seconds. A faint, grudging nod of approval crossed the old man's face.

'Good,' Ramakant-ji said. 'Take the train tomorrow morning.'

'The branch line is under gauge conversion,' Madhav said. 'I will rent a vehicle. And I will take Divya.'

The room went completely silent. The junior from Hardoi held his breath.

Nirmala Devi, who had just entered the baithak with a plate of sliced betel nut, stopped by the doorway. 'Take Divya? To a village near the forest? What will she do in a revenue dispute?'

Madhav looked at his mother. Then he looked at Divya, who was standing frozen by the pantry steps, the empty brass tray pressed against her ribs.

'Her uncle's family has an old guest lease near the forest rest house,' Madhav said, holding his mother's gaze without blinking. 'She has not left this house in eight months, Amma. She is coming with me.'

storySections.chapterTitle: III. The Road to the Grassland
storySections.heading: III. The Road to the Grassland
storySections.body:
They left Qaiserbagh at 5:00 on a Saturday morning, while the streetlamps were still burning through the mist.

Madhav had rented an old olive-green Mahindra Thar from a transport contractor in Gomti Nagar. It was ten years old, with a mechanical transfer case that whined in third gear, leaf springs that squeaked over every pothole, and seats covered in worn black vinyl that smelled of dust and diesel fuel.

It was the antithesis of the family's chauffeured white sedan.

Divya sat in the passenger seat. She had changed out of her silk handloom saree into an old pair of dark grey canvas trousers and a faded navy fleece jacket she had pulled from the very bottom of her second trunk.

Beside her feet, sitting on the rubber floor mat, was the black canvas case containing the Nikon binoculars.

For the first two hours, neither of them spoke.

The Thar rattled north along State Highway 25, cutting through the vast, flat agricultural heartland of central Uttar Pradesh. On either side of the road, endless fields of winter sugarcane rose ten feet into the grey sky, their feathery purple tassels nodding in the morning wind. At Sitapur, they stopped at a roadside dhaba where three truck drivers sat on wooden cot frames drinking sweet tea from clay cups.

Madhav ordered two earthen kullads of tea and a plate of hot dal kachoris fried in mustard oil.

He set the clay cup on the wooden table before her.

Divya took the cup between both palms. Her fingers were cold. She looked at the road—at the tractors hauling cane to the sugar mill, the bullock carts with red reflectors on their axles, the wide, unpaved horizons of the north.

'There is no revenue dispute in Palia Kalan, is there, Madhav?' she asked quietly.

Madhav took a sip of his tea. The ginger burned his tongue.

'No,' he said.

'Why did you bring me here?'

Madhav looked at his hands. For seven years, he had operated inside courtroom chambers where language was an instrument of strategic ambiguity—where every word was weighed for its liability, its evidentiary burden, its procedural risk.

Now, sitting on a greasy wooden cot thirty miles from the Nepal border, the legal vocabulary felt utterly useless.

'Because you were disappearing, Divya,' he said.

She looked up. Her eyes, wide and startled, met his.

'I was watching you in my father's house,' Madhav continued, his voice barely louder than the hum of the tea stall's kerosene stove. 'You make tea. You slice almonds. You answer my mother with two words: *Ji, Amma*. You fold the laundry. You don't read your journals. You haven't mentioned your thesis in two years. You walk through the courtyard like someone who has committed a crime and is waiting for the sentence to be carried out.'

Divya's lower lip trembled. She looked down at the clay cup in her hands.

'I am trying to be a good wife, Madhav,' she whispered. 'Your family has a status. Your father has a reputation. I didn't want to be the woman who broke the harmony of your home.'

'That isn't harmony, Divya,' Madhav said, reaching across the rough wooden table and covering her cold fingers with his palm. 'That is an occupation. My father doesn't want harmony; he wants obedience. And I was so cowardly, so terrified of his disappointment, that I let him demand it from you.'

A tear detached from her lash and fell into the steaming tea.

'I thought you wanted me to be like her,' she said, her voice cracking. 'I thought that was the price of being married to you.'

'If I wanted a woman like my mother, Divya,' Madhav said, his voice fierce and trembling with an emotion he had never permitted himself to feel inside the Qaiserbagh walls, 'I would not have stood behind that temple pillar at Allahabad for forty minutes watching you talk to the river birds. I fell in love with a woman who had mud on her boots and fire in her mind. And I have spent four years watching that fire drown in eight-ounce teacups.'

He stood up, dropped a fifty-rupee note onto the wooden table, and walked around to open her car door.

'Drink your tea,' he said gently. 'We have thirty miles before the forest gate. The swamp deer feed before noon.'

storySections.chapterTitle: IV. The Mist over the Suheli
storySections.heading: IV. The Mist over the Suheli
storySections.body:
They crossed the railway crossing at Mailani and entered Dudhwa National Park at 9:30 AM.

The transition from the agricultural plains to the Terai forest was instantaneous and absolute. The sugarcane gave way to colossal, eighty-foot sal trees whose straight, grey trunks rose like the pillars of an ancient Gothic cathedral, their dark foliage knitting together overhead to block the winter sun.

The air dropped five degrees in two hundred meters. It smelled of damp fallen leaves, wild turmeric, wet clay, and the rich, pungent scent of elephant dung along the grassy verges.

Divya rolled her window all the way down.

She leaned her head against the frame, closing her eyes. She inhaled the air with deep, shuddering breaths—the air of her youth, uncurrupted by city carbon or domestic coal smoke.

Madhav turned the Thar off the main tarmac road onto an unpaved forest patrol track that ran along the northern levee of the Suheli river. The vehicle bounced and groaned through deep ruts dried into grey mud, the yellow grass scraping against the doors with a dry, hissing sound.

Two miles inside the grassland buffer, Divya suddenly grabbed his forearm.

'Stop,' she whispered.

Her voice had changed. The hesitant, muted tone of the Qaiserbagh daughter-in-law had vanished. It was low, crisp, and authoritative.

Madhav cut the engine. The mechanical shudder died, leaving only the colossal, ringing silence of the forest—the high, electric whistle of cicadas in the sal canopy, the distant gurgle of the river, and the dry rustle of wind through ten-foot elephant grass.

Divya reached down, unzipped the black canvas case with one smooth motion, and pulled out the Nikon field binoculars.

She adjusted the central diopter ring with her thumb. She lifted the heavy black barrels to her eyes, bracing her elbows against the Thar's open window frame.

Her posture had completely transformed. The bowed shoulders, the guarded, self-effacing curve of her spine was gone. Her neck was taut, her chin lifted, her eyes focused with predatory, scientific concentration.

'Look,' she whispered, pointing with her left index finger toward a broad, shallow bend in the river two hundred meters to the northwest. 'Between the two cotton trees. Near the water hyacinth.'

Madhav squinted through the windshield. At first, he saw only the flat expanse of grey water and the yellow reeds.

Then the reeds moved.

Stepping out of the tall grass into the shallow water was a herd of nine swamp deer—the Barasingha.

They were magnificent. The dominant stag stood five feet tall at the shoulder, his coat a rich, golden chestnut, his head crowned with a colossal, twelve-pointed rack of dark antlers that swept back over his spine like an ornamental throne. Behind him moved six hinds and two half-grown fawns, their hooves splashing silently in the shallow marsh as they dipped their muzzles into the water hyacinth.

Divya watched them for ten minutes without lowering the glasses.

A faint, brilliant flush had risen into her cheeks. Her lips were parted slightly; she was murmuring observations under her breath in a rhythmic, scientific shorthand:

*'Adult male, prime condition, rack complete, twelve tines. Three lactating females. The corridor between the river bend and the railway line is still active. The encroachment hasn't broken the migration path yet...'*

She lowered the binoculars. She turned toward Madhav.

Her face was illuminated from within. The dark, lifeless veil that had covered her features for four years had been stripped away. In its place was the woman he had fallen in love with at Allahabad—brilliant, formidable, and entirely alive.

She looked at him. Her eyes filled with tears, but they were not the tears of the teacups.

'They're still here, Madhav,' she whispered, her voice trembling with awe. 'They're still here.'

'I know,' Madhav said softly. 'And so are you.'

storySections.heading: V. The Veranda at Dudhwa
storySections.body:
They spent the night at the Sonaripur Forest Rest House, an old colonial timber bungalow built on five-foot brick stilts on the edge of the grassland.

The room had a stone fireplace where the forest guard burned dry sal logs, two iron cot beds with thick wool blankets, and an old teak writing desk beside a bay window looking into the forest.

At dawn, before the mist had burned off the grass, they sat on the wooden veranda in two cane armchairs.

A guard had brought them two glasses of black tea with crushed ginger and wild honey in a metal pot.

The world was entirely white. A dense, silver-grey Terai mist clung to the ground, rising five feet into the air, so that the distant trees looked like islands floating in an ocean of milk. Above the mist, the rising sun was a pale orange disc, casting long, coppery reflections across the dew-soaked grass.

Divya held her glass between her palms.

'What happens when we go back on Monday, Madhav?' she asked.

The question was calm, but beneath it lay the entire weight of their future.

'We do not go back to what it was,' Madhav said.

He turned his chair toward her.

'I have three files of independent practice,' he said. 'Cases I brought in myself, without Babuji's chamber. Two title arbitrations in Gomti Nagar and an environmental writ petition challenging industrial effluent discharge into the Gomti river. The fees are enough to rent a floor in Indira Nagar.'

Divya stared at him, her eyes wide. 'Leave Qaiserbagh? Madhav, your father will never forgive you. He will say I corrupted you. He will say I destroyed his family.'

'My father survived forty years of civil litigation,' Madhav said, his voice steady, cold, and clear. 'He will survive a son who rents an apartment two miles away.'

He reached across the space between the cane chairs and took her right hand. He looked down at the two thin gold bangles that had clicked against the chopping board for four years.

'You finish your thesis, Divya,' he said. 'You apply for the research fellowship at the Terai Ecological Foundation. You spend your winters here in Dudhwa, running your transects and tracking your deer. And when you come home to Lucknow, you come home to a house where you are the master of your own mind, not a servant in someone else's court.'

Divya began to weep.

She wept with her head resting against his shoulder, her tears soaking through the sleeve of his dark wool sweater. It was the release of four years of compressed breath—the terrifying, magnificent collapse of the cage she had built around her own heart to keep from dying of shame.

Madhav held her. He rested his chin against her hair, smelling the smoke of the sal logs and the wild river air.

A marriage, he realized, was not a contract of mutual surrender.

It was not two people agreeing to become less than themselves so that their families could remain comfortable. A real marriage was a conspiracy. It was a secret, enduring alliance between two people to protect each other's vitality against the immense, grinding weight of the world's conventions.

If he could not be the advocate who saved his wife from his own father's house, then every legal argument he had ever made before the High Court was nothing more than empty noise.

storySections.chapterTitle: VI. The Binoculars on the Cedar Desk
storySections.heading: VI. The Binoculars on the Cedar Desk
storySections.body:
They returned to Lucknow at six on Sunday evening.

The Thar pulled into the gravel driveway of the Qaiserbagh house, its olive-green panels splattered to the roofline with dry grey Terai mud.

In the central courtyard, the grandfather clock struck the half-hour with its bronze, mechanical gong.

Ramakant-ji was sitting on the wicker sofa in the inner veranda, drinking tea from a porcelain cup, reading the weekend law reports. Nirmala Devi sat beside him, shelling fresh peas into a brass colander.

When the heavy wooden front door opened, both of them looked up.

Madhav walked in first, carrying his leather briefcase.

Behind him came Divya.

She was still wearing her dark canvas trousers and her fleece jacket, her hiking boots leaving faint prints of dried forest mud on the white marble floor of the vestibule.

She was not carrying a tea tray.

In her right hand, held firmly by the leather neck strap, were the black Nikon binoculars. The lenses were uncapped; the black rubber barrels were scratched with yellow pollen from the elephant grass.

Nirmala Devi froze. Her hands, holding a half-opened pea pod, remained suspended above the brass colander.

Ramakant-ji lowered his reading glasses. He looked at Divya's trousers. He looked at the mud on the marble. Then he looked at the black binoculars in her hand.

'Divya,' Ramakant-ji said, his voice carrying the deep, resonant authority that had silenced three hundred courtrooms. 'What is that?'

Divya did not bow her head.

She did not pull her pallu over her collarbone, and she did not look down at the floor.

She stood in the center of the marble lightwell, directly beneath the swinging pendulum of the Birmingham clock. She looked straight into the eyes of the most formidable lawyer in the state of Uttar Pradesh.

'These are my field glasses, Babuji,' she said. Her voice was quiet, polite, and entirely unyielding. 'I have been cataloging the swamp deer population along the Suheli corridor. I will be submitting my research proposal to the state wildlife board on Friday.'

Ramakant-ji's mouth opened slightly. For three seconds, the senior advocate of the Oudh Bar had no response.

He turned his gaze toward his son.

'Madhav,' he said, his voice dropping an octave into an icy, dangerous register. 'What is the meaning of this?'

Madhav stepped forward. He stood beside his wife.

He did not apologize, and he did not raise his voice. He reached down, took Divya's left hand in his, and interlaced his fingers with hers.

'It means Divya is an ecologist, Babuji,' Madhav said, looking at his father with calm, steady eyes. 'And tomorrow morning, we are looking at flats in Indira Nagar.'

The silence in the courtyard was absolute.

For a long time, the only sound in the house was the swinging of the Birmingham pendulum: *tick, tock, tick, tock*.

Ramakant-ji stared at his son. He stared at their joined hands. The anger rose into the old man's face, turning his temples crimson; then, as he looked at Madhav's eyes—at the stubborn, unshakeable jawline he had passed down to his boy thirty years ago—the anger stalled.

He recognized the posture.

It was the posture of an advocate who had prepared his brief, verified his authorities, and was prepared to take the matter all the way to the Supreme Court.

Ramakant-ji looked back down at his law report.

He did not shout. He did not bless them. He merely turned a page with a sharp rustle of heavy paper.

'The roof of the Indira Nagar house,' Ramakant-ji murmured, not looking up from the text, 'leaks in July. Check the terrace waterproofing before you sign the lease.'

Divya looked at Madhav.

A small, secret smile passed between them—a smile forged in the mist of the northern forests, tested against the traditions of an ancient house, and found indestructible.

Divya walked up the wooden stairs to their bedroom.

She did not open the bottom shelf of the wardrobe, and she did not hide the black case behind the wool quilts.

She walked to the cedar writing desk beside the window. She cleared away two piles of old legal magazines, set the black binoculars down in the center of the polished wood, and opened the window to let the evening air of the city in.
